About Your Privacy

We process your data to deliver content or advertisements and measure the delivery of such content or advertisements to extract insights about our website. We share this information with our partners on the basis of consent and legitimate interest. You may exercise your right to consent or object to a legitimate interest, based on a specific purpose below or at a partner level in the link under each purpose. These choices will be signaled to our vendors participating in the Transparency and Consent Framework and saved in a cookie on your device called “fides_consent” for a maximum duration of 12 months.

Below, you will find a list of the purposes and special features for which your data is being processed. You may exercise your rights for specific purposes, based on consent or legitimate interest, using the toggles below.
Purposes
Audience Measurement
On

We use audience measurement cookies in order to carry out aggregated traffic measurement and generate performance statistics essential for the proper functioning of the site and the provision of its content (for example to measure performance, to detect navigation problems, to optimization technical performance or ergonomics, to estimate server power needed and to analyse content performance). The use of these cookies is strictly limited to measuring the site's audience. These cookies do not allow the tracking of navigation on other websites and the data collected is not combined or shared with third parties. You can refuse the use of this cookie by switching off the slider to the right.

Essential
On

This website uses essential cookies and services to enable core website functionality and provide a seamless user experience. These cookies and services are used to facilitate features such as navigation, remembering user references, and ensuring website security.

Functional Cookies
On

These cookies enable the website to provide enhanced functionality and personalisation. They may be set by us or by third party providers whose services we have added to our pages. If you do not allow these cookies then some or all of these services may not function properly.

Targeted Advertising
On

These cookies may be set through our site by our advertising partners. They may be used by those companies to build a profile of your interests and show you relevant adverts on other sites. They do not store directly personal information, but are based on uniquely identifying your browser and internet device. If you do not allow these cookies, you will experience less targeted advertising.

Performance Cookies
On

These cookies allow us to count visits and traffic sources so we can measure and improve the performance of our site. They help us to know which pages are the most and least popular and see how visitors move around the site. All information these cookies collect is aggregated and therefore anonymous. If you do not allow these cookies we will not know when you have visited our site, and will not be able to monitor its performance.

Social Media Cookies
On

These cookies are set by a range of social media services that we have added to the site to enable you to share our content with your friends and networks. They are capable of tracking your browser across other sites and building up a profile of your interests. This may impact the content and messages you see on other websites you visit. If you do not allow these cookies you may not be able to use or see these sharing tools.

Store and/or access information on a device
On
IAB TCF

Cookies, device or similar online identifiers (e.g. login-based identifiers, randomly assigned identifiers, network based identifiers) together with other information (e.g. browser type and information, language, screen size, supported technologies etc.) can be stored or read on your device to recognise it each time it connects to an app or to a website, for one or several of the purposes presented here.

Most purposes explained in this notice rely on the storage or accessing of information from your device when you use an app or visit a website. For example, a vendor or publisher might need to store a cookie on your device during your first visit on a website, to be able to recognise your device during your next visits (by accessing this cookie each time).

Use limited data to select advertising

IAB TCF

Advertising presented to you on this service can be based on limited data, such as the website or app you are using, your non-precise location, your device type or which content you are (or have been) interacting with (for example, to limit the number of times an ad is presented to you).

A car manufacturer wants to promote its electric vehicles to environmentally conscious users living in the city after office hours. The advertising is presented on a page with related content (such as an article on climate change actions) after 6:30 p.m. to users whose non-precise location suggests that they are in an urban zone.

A large producer of watercolour paints wants to carry out an online advertising campaign for its latest watercolour range, diversifying its audience to reach as many amateur and professional artists as possible and avoiding showing the ad next to mismatched content (for instance, articles about how to paint your house). The number of times that the ad has been presented to you is detected and limited, to avoid presenting it too often.

Create profiles for personalised advertising

IAB TCF

Information about your activity on this service (such as forms you submit, content you look at) can be stored and combined with other information about you (for example, information from your previous activity on this service and other websites or apps) or similar users. This is then used to build or improve a profile about you (that might include possible interests and personal aspects). Your profile can be used (also later) to present advertising that appears more relevant based on your possible interests by this and other entities.

If you read several articles about the best bike accessories to buy, this information could be used to create a profile about your interest in bike accessories. Such a profile may be used or improved later on, on the same or a different website or app to present you with advertising for a particular bike accessory brand. If you also look at a configurator for a vehicle on a luxury car manufacturer website, this information could be combined with your interest in bikes to refine your profile and make an assumption that you are interested in luxury cycling gear.

An apparel company wishes to promote its new line of high-end baby clothes. It gets in touch with an agency that has a network of clients with high income customers (such as high-end supermarkets) and asks the agency to create profiles of young parents or couples who can be assumed to be wealthy and to have a new child, so that these can later be used to present advertising within partner apps based on those profiles.

Inside jeweller Celia Weinstock’s Chelsea townhouse designed around art, antiques and the pleasures of small rooms

Bucking the trend for open-plan living, Guy Goodfellow transformed a once unloved and dilapidated house into an elegant family home, with intimate, country-house interiors inspired by Celia's inherited family paintings
By Amy BradfordPhotography by Christopher Horwood
2 October 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:05
Instaread

‘We have definitely reacted against open-plan living,’ says Celia Weinstock of the Chelsea townhouse she shares with her husband Max Benitz and their two infant sons. Aside from a combined kitchen, dining and sitting room on the lower-ground floor, their four-bedroom home is in complete contrast to that approach. ‘It’s mainly comprised of small rooms where we all have private spaces,’ says Celia, who is an investor. ‘I love the layout, and we use all the rooms, which is very satisfying.’

In fact, the five-storey home’s celebration of intimate rooms is not the only way it bucks modern convention. Built around 1850, it would once have had a formal parlour, but Celia and Max chose to dispense with this in favour of more characterful spaces, such as a library, a small room with a bar overlooking the garden, and his and hers studies. ‘We were happy to sacrifice having the typical Victorian double reception, as we use the drawing room only for entertaining,’ explains Celia. Instead, the focal point of the ground floor is a central hall leading off the staircase, lined with a mix of real and faux books, and anchored by a striking marble fireplace. The space is as practical as it is charming.

‘The idea behind it was to have a large enough space to store outdoor coats, shoes and a buggy,’ says Celia. ‘We also wanted it to make a strong stylistic statement, as it’s the first room you see when you enter the house.’ The couple enlisted Alexander Smith of A&A Architects to renovate the building, and designer Guy Goodfellow to oversee the interiors. The two collaborated to create the central hall, fulfilling the couple’s wish for a blend of functionality and visual impact.

Advertisement

‘The open bookcases are interspersed with jibbed cupboards concealing wardrobes,’ says Guy. ‘A tall opening links to the intimate drawing room and also to the well-lit bar space, which feels almost like a garden room during the day, and atmospheric and clublike in the evenings.’

When Celia and Max bought the house, it was dilapidated and had lost many of its original features; it was also unlisted. ‘This gave us the opportunity to reinvent the house to suit the way they wanted to live,’ says Guy. ‘The brief was to create a luxurious backdrop for everyday life and entertaining.’ The architects dug down at basement level to achieve a generous 3.2-metre ceiling height, and an ‘uninspiring’ timber staircase was replaced with a sweeping cantilevered stone design. In addition, Guy and Alexander enhanced the architectural details, adding chunky cornices and installing chimneypieces by Jamb to make the house feel more like its grand original self.

Celia and Guy have naturally aligned tastes. ‘I chose him partly because I adore his eponymous fabric and wallpaper collection,’ Celia enthuses. ‘He is particularly gifted with colour palettes.’ The English country-house look she loves is made to feel modern through subtle hues and unexpected pattern combinations. This, adds Guy, ‘makes this Chelsea townhouse feel more impressive than its size should dictate’. Throughout, his own designs are juxtaposed with creations from heritage makers. In the bar, blinds in his ‘Tangier’ weave contrast with Pierre Frey’s ‘Fontainebleau’ botanical wallpaper, while in the library, de Gournay’s ‘India Tea Paper’ wallcovering in a soft straw shade complements curtains in Guy’s gold ‘Persian Vine’ fabric.

Advertisement

Other deft touches make entertaining a joy. ‘The drinks bar incorporates a wine fridge and a sink – useful in a tall London townhouse in which the kitchen is on the floor below – and the banquette sofa is intended for a couple of friends to gather and gossip, away from the social group,’ Guy explains. ‘In order to allow enough people to be seated in the drawing room, we decided to build a window seat. We added a blind and converted the original shutters, painting and lacquering them to resemble Chinese screens. They never fail to enchant visitors.’

Art was the starting point of the whole design. ‘I inherited Old Masters and antiques from my family, so that dictated the look of the house,’ says Celia. ‘I grew up with these pieces, so they have sentimental value. Many people like to add art and furniture to their house over time, and recommend living there first before renovating; we took the opposite approach. The rooms were designed around all the art, furniture and lighting that we had in storage.’ Every painting and object was measured and added to the architectural drawings before renovations began. As a result, the couple were able to move into the house only 15 months later, in summer 2024. Celia’s favourite space remains the unusual (but invaluable) central hall. ‘We wanted it to have a grand country-house feel with the fireplace, the books and some horse-racing trophies I inherited,’ she says. ‘We also wanted it to feel quite masculine, as it was designed around the portrait of my husband’s great-grandfather in his RAF uniform above the chimneypiece. We are thrilled with the result – it’s such an elegant storage solution’.
